tagline: River pilings mark the timber trade beside a north-flowing river
intro: The Pend Oreille Valley Scenic Byway follows Highway 20 between Tiger and Newport, beside a river flowing north toward Canada. Scenic Washington presents this stretch as Washington’s southernmost leg of the International Selkirk Loop, with river history and forest recreation among its attractions. Pilings remain in the water from log-holding areas that supplied the Diamond Match mill at Cusick. The river runs along the eastern side of the Selkirk Mountains; its terrain grows more rugged toward the north, beyond the valley’s southern reaches.

Automobiles changed a valley whose settlements had depended on riverboats and railroads. Newport newspaper editor Fred L. Wolf campaigned for better roads and a bridge across the Pend Oreille. Governor Ernest Lister vetoed a proposed bridge in 1913; a crossing finally opened in 1927, improving travel between northeastern Washington and northern Idaho. That bridge was replaced in 1989.

Traveling south starts at Tiger’s Highway 20/31 junction, where the former general store and post office houses a historical center. The sequence continues through Cusick and Usk, with the Kalispel Tribe’s Reservation across the river from Usk. Newport finishes the drive at the meeting of Highway 20 and U.S. 2, beside the Idaho state line.

moments.title: Cusick
moments.text: River pilings survive from the log-boom holding areas that supplied Cusick’s Diamond Match mill. Western white pine forests supplied its timber at the turn of the century. Cusick was founded by Joseph W. Cusick in 1902 and incorporated in 1927. The town also serves as headquarters of the Kalispel Indian Community of the Kalispel Reservation.
moments.notice: Pilings in the river mark former log-boom holding areas.

moments.title: Usk
moments.text: Across the river from Usk, the Kalispel Tribe manages a buffalo herd visible from LeClerc Road. The community itself takes its name from the River Usk in Wales, a name adopted around 1890. It lies two miles southeast of Cusick along the Pend Oreille River.

moments.title: Newport
moments.text: A straight state line separates Newport from Oldtown, Idaho, with no natural or physical barrier between them. The original Newport settlement stood on the Idaho side, where river transportation supported trade. The Great Northern Railway arrived in 1892, and the Washington community grew into the principal town. On Washington Avenue, plaques identify earlier businesses and their dates. At the street’s end, Centennial Plaza commemorates Washington’s state centennial, another boundary story made visible in the town. The county historical museum brings buildings from different places together, including three log cabins dismantled and reconstructed on its grounds.
